turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you here today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yeah, thank you for seeing me. Um, so, I guess the main thing that finally pushed me to come in—and it took me a while to actually make the appointment, honestly, because I kept putting it off—but the main issue is with my job. I work as an insurance claims processing clerk. I've been doing it for a bit since I left college, and it's, you know, it's a lot of computer work. You sit at a workstation and you just go through these policy files and claim reviews one after another. 

And the thing is, I just keep getting up from my workstation during the day. Like, constantly. I know I’m supposed to stay put, I really do. I’ll look at my monitor and think, "Okay, you have to sit here and finish these claim reviews before lunch," but the next thing I know, I'm out of my chair. I’m wandering over to the breakroom, or I'm walking down the hall, or I'm just standing up and pacing around the cubicles for way too long. And it's not like I'm trying to avoid work on purpose or be rebellious or anything, it's just... I can't seem to just stay in my seat. It’s getting to be a real problem because the claims just pile up, and I know I need to just sit there and finish them, but I just keep leaving my desk anyway.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they constantly get up from their workstation and wander around or pace, despite knowing they are supposed to stay seated to finish their work.

turns.doctor_question: Do you feel this happens because you’re deliberately resisting directions or authority, or does it feel unintentional?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, it's definitely not that. I mean, I'm not trying to be a rebel or stick it to the man or anything like that. I actually really respect my supervisor, Linda. She's been very patient with me, all things considered. It's more like... it's completely unintentional. I’ll be sitting there, right? And I’ll have a stack of, say, auto collision claims open on my dual monitors—because they give us two monitors so we can cross-reference the policy details with the adjuster's notes—and I’ll be looking right at the screen, knowing I need to hit 'approve' or 'flag for review' by 3:00 PM. I know the rules. I know the expectations. 

But then, it's almost like my brain just bypasses the part where I make a conscious decision to stay. I’ll think, "Oh, my water bottle is empty," or "I should just stretch my legs for one second," and before I even realize I've made a choice, I'm already halfway down the hall near the printer. And I don't even need anything from the printer! I just end up there. Or I'll find myself talking to Dave in accounting about his weekend, and in the back of my head, I'm thinking, "You need to be at your desk, you have 15 claims left in the queue," but I just can't seem to make myself turn around and sit back down in that chair. It’s frustrating because I want to do a good job, I really do, but it just feels like my body is acting on its own sometimes, you know? Like I'm just floating away from my desk without even meaning to.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly describes unintentionally leaving their desk and wandering down the hall when they are expected to remain seated and work on claims.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also have trouble staying focused on tasks or conversations even when you’re trying to pay attention?
turns.patient_response:
Um, no, actually, I don't think so. I haven't really noticed anything like that. Like, if I'm actually trying to pay attention, I'm pretty good at it. Take conversations, for example. When I was talking to Dave—like I mentioned just a second ago, from accounting—he was telling me this incredibly long story about his weekend, because he went up to this lake about two hours north of here. Lake... oh, I can't remember the exact name, but it's famous for trout fishing. Anyway, he was going on and on about the specific type of lure he was using, and the weather, and how his outboard motor was acting up, and I heard every single word. I wasn't zoning out at all. I was completely following along. Even when I know in the back of my head that I should be back at my desk, I'm still entirely focused on what he's saying to me. 

And it's the exact same with the claims themselves. When I'm actually sitting in front of my monitors, and I'm reading through a complex liability file, I don't lose my place or forget what I'm reading. I can read the adjuster's notes perfectly fine and process all the information. I know exactly what the policy limits are, whether the deductible was met, all of that. It’s not that my mind wanders off the task itself or that I can't concentrate on the words in front of me, it's just that... well, like I said, I end up physically wandering away from the workstation. But the actual focus part? No, if I'm looking at a document or listening to someone speak, I'm locked in. I haven't had any complaints about not listening when people talk to me, except maybe from my mom sometimes when I go over for dinner, but you know how that is, mothers always think you aren't listening to them. But at work, or when I'm trying? No, my focus on the actual work or conversations is completely fine.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient admits that they end up physically wandering away from their workstation.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly denies having trouble staying focused on tasks or conversations, stating they are 'locked in' and their focus is 'completely fine'.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient denies having complaints about not listening when people talk to them, stating they hear every word.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often make careless mistakes or miss details when you're doing work or other tasks?
turns.patient_response:
Um, no, actually. No, I wouldn't say that at all. It's kind of funny you ask that, because if anything, I might be almost too careful when I'm actually looking at the files. We have this quality assurance team at my company—they sit up on the third floor, and they randomly pull, I think it's about five percent of our processed claims every single week just to audit them for accuracy. They check for coding errors, missed deductibles, whether we applied the right depreciation rules, all that stuff. And my QA scores are always really, really high. 

Like, I don't miss the small stuff. If I'm reviewing a file for, let's say, a multi-vehicle collision, I have to cross-reference the police report with the insured's statement and the field adjuster's estimate. And you have to look at all these tiny details, right? Like the 17-digit VIN numbers, the exact time of the accident, whether there was a lapse in coverage that month... and I catch all of that. I'll sit there and verify every single line item on the estimate. I'm really meticulous about making sure the software calculated everything correctly. 

So I'm definitely not making careless mistakes. The work I actually get done is practically perfect, honestly. I don't gloss over things or rush through and mess up. It's just... well, like I was trying to explain earlier, the problem isn't the quality of the work or me missing details, it's just the quantity. Because I end up walking away from my monitors so much, my overall numbers are low. But no, when I'm actually working on a claim, my attention to detail is totally fine. I don't really make errors like that.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions walking away from their monitors so much that their overall productivity is low, indicating they frequently leave their seat.
symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly denies making careless mistakes or missing details, emphasizing that their work is meticulous and highly accurate.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often misplace important things, like your keys, phone, or paperwork?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, man. Yeah. Yes, absolutely. That... that is definitely a huge problem for me. It's actually incredibly frustrating, because, like I said, I'm so careful with the actual data on the computer, but in the physical world? I am constantly—and I mean constantly—hunting for things I literally just had in my hand two seconds prior. 

For instance, at work, we have these headsets, right? Because we have to take calls from the field adjusters or sometimes the insured parties if there's a dispute about the settlement amount. And they're wireless headsets, which is supposed to be convenient, but for me, it's a nightmare. I’ll take it off for a second to go get that water I mentioned, or to go to the bathroom, and when I come back to my desk, it's just gone. And I'll spend ten minutes tearing apart my cubicle, looking under the keyboard, behind the monitors, in my drawers, only to find I somehow left it on top of the filing cabinet by the breakroom. 

And it's not just the headset. It's paperwork, too. We're mostly paperless, but sometimes we get physical mail, like a police report that someone mailed in instead of faxing or emailing. I'll have a physical claim form in my hand, I'll set it down to type something, and then poof. It's vanished. I'll be shuffling through stacks of blank printer paper, lifting up my mouse pad, checking the trash can just in case I accidentally threw it away. 

Sticky notes are the worst, though. I'll write down a really important callback number—like, say, an adjuster leaves a voicemail and says, "Hey, call me back at this specific extension," and I'll write it on a yellow sticky note. I'll stick it right to the bezel of my monitor. But then later, when I actually need to make the call, the sticky note isn't there. Did it fall off? Did it stick to the bottom of my coffee mug? Did I peel it off and stick it to my forehead without realizing? I have no idea. 

And my access badge! Oh, my god, my access badge. We need it to get into the building, to get onto the elevator, to get through the glass doors on our floor. It's on a retractable lanyard that clips to my belt. But somehow, I manage to unclip it, set it down somewhere—maybe on my desk, maybe in the bathroom, maybe on Dave's desk in accounting—and then I'm locked out of my own department. I've had to have security print me a temporary badge, like, four times this month alone. The security guard, Greg, he just shakes his head at me now when he sees me walking up to the desk. It's embarrassing, really. It just feels like everything I touch just evaporates the second I look away.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly confirms constantly losing important items necessary for tasks, such as their work headset, physical claim forms, sticky notes with callback numbers, and their building access badge.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have these kinds of attention or organization problems back when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yeah. Yeah, definitely. Looking back on it now, this whole thing isn't exactly brand new for me. It's actually been going on for a really, really long time. 

I actually remember—my mom kept all my old report cards from elementary school in this big plastic tote bin in the basement, and we went through it a couple of years ago when she was downsizing and moving out of my childhood home. And it was honestly kind of wild to read them, because it was just so consistent. Every single year, from like first grade all the way up through middle school, the teachers would write the exact same kind of comments in that little 'teacher notes' section at the bottom of the page. 

They would always start off by saying that I was a really bright kid, you know? "He's very bright, he has so much potential"—that was the classic line they all used. But then it would immediately be followed by this laundry list of issues. They were constantly writing about how I lost my worksheets. And it was true! My backpack was like a total black hole. I would actually do the homework at my kitchen table, I swear I did, but by the time I got to school the next morning, it was just gone. Crumbled at the very bottom under a gym shirt, or left on the kitchen counter, or I'd somehow accidentally thrown it away with my lunch bag. 

And they'd also always mention how I missed instructions. Like, the teacher would stand at the front of the room and explain a whole science activity, and everyone else would pull out their materials and get right to work, and I'd just be sitting there, having to lean over and ask the kid next to me what we were supposed to be doing because the instructions just completely flew over my head. 

And then there was the classwork itself. I was always the last one done, not because I didn't understand the material—like I said, I got the actual concepts—but because I just needed constant reminders to actually finish the work in front of me. I remember Mrs. Higgins in third grade, she used to literally walk by my desk every ten minutes and just tap her pen on my paper to get me to keep writing. If she didn't do that, I'd just be staring at the wall or fiddling with my erasers. 

So, yeah, I guess when you really look at it, this whole pattern of losing things and needing to be constantly redirected to finish what I'm doing... it's been happening since I was a little kid. It's just that back then, the stakes were a spelling worksheet, and now the stakes are my career and my performance metrics, you know? But the actual behavior? Oh, absolutely, it was definitely there in elementary school. My mom used to get so frustrated at those parent-teacher conferences, I can still picture her face when we'd walk out of the classroom...

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes needing constant reminders to finish classwork and staring at the wall instead of working, indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly states they missed instructions and failed to finish schoolwork without constant redirection.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports a long-standing pattern of losing worksheets and homework, describing their backpack as a 'black hole'.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient mentions 'fiddling with my erasers' when not being actively redirected to their work.
